facts.fact: Name for the term: "vây đuôi"
Name for the term: "caudal fin"
The caudal fin is the tail fin, at the end of the caudal peduncle; the name comes from the Latin cauda, meaning tail.
In most fish groups the caudal fin is used for propulsion: fish get thrust by moving the vertical tail fin from side to side.
The caudal fin is supported by the vertebrae of the axial skeleton and by pterygiophores (radials).
Most modern teleosts have a homocercal tail: it looks mostly symmetrical, and the vertebrae run only a short way into the upper lobe.
In a heterocercal tail the vertebrae extend into the upper lobe, which is often longer than the lower lobe, as in sharks and sturgeons.
In a diphycercal tail the vertebrae reach the tip of a symmetrical, expanded tail, as in bichirs, lungfish and coelacanths.

Homocercal tail shapes are rounded, truncate (a roughly vertical edge, as in trout), emarginate (slightly curved in, as in Eurasian carp, Cyprinus carpio), forked (as in catla) or lunate (crescent-shaped, as in swordfish).
"Đuôi đơn" is the general term for domesticated bettas (Betta) whose tail has only one lobe; veiltail, delta, superdelta, halfmoon and roundtail are single-tail forms.
"Plakat" is the name for short-tailed bettas (Betta); young males can be hard to tell from females.
"Đuôi voan (veiltail)": the tail is balanced, wide at the base and extended at the edge.
"Cá betta đuôi màn / Veiltail": a betta (Betta) with a long, drooping caudal fin.
"Đuôi quạt (roundtail)": the tail is round, and this form often turns up in delta, superdelta and halfmoon lines.
"Delta": a triangular betta (Betta) tail with long rays and often-curved edges; the page gives its spread both as under 160 degrees and as 160 to 179 degrees.
"Superdelta": a betta (Betta) tail that spreads between 160 and 180 degrees.
"Halfmoon": a betta (Betta) tail with straight rays that spreads a full 180 degrees; a wider spread is called over halfmoon (oHM).
"Halfmoon": the traits come from several genes, so fish in a spawn that lack one or two of them may be classed as delta or superdelta.
"Cá betta halfmoon": a large, wide caudal fin that spreads at about 180 degrees; the ventral and anal fins are also longer than in other betta (Betta) lines.
"Cá betta halfmoon": fairly aggressive, especially the males.
"Đuôi hoa (rosetail)": bred by selecting halfmoon bettas (Betta) whose rays branch and stick out in bud-like clusters.
"Cá betta rosetail": its fins are so wide that they wrinkle at the edges, and it can open its tail more than 180 degrees.
"Cá betta rosetail": its very large fins and tail often cause swimming problems.
"Đuôi tưa (crowntail)": a betta (Betta) whose fin rays extend past the edge of the tail like a crown; ray patterns are single, double, triple and double-double.
"Cá betta đuôi tưa / Crowntail": split fins form many thin, pointed, long tail sections that look like a palm leaf.
"Cá betta đuôi tưa / Crowntail": more prone to tail disease and somewhat more aggressive than other betta (Betta) lines.
"Cá betta Combtail": looks like a crowntail, but the split parts are no longer than half of the total tail length.
"Đuôi kép (doubletail)": a betta (Betta) with two tail lobes and a much larger than normal dorsal fin; the lobes should be equal and split to the base.
"Cá betta đuôi kép/ Doubletail": the tail splits into two separate parts.
"Đuôi ba thuỳ (tripletail)": a rare betta (Betta) tail with three lobes.
"Đuôi tim (hearttail)": a rare betta (Betta) tail whose two lobes split only partly, making a heart shape; breeding often gives fully split doubletails instead.
"Đuôi dính (fusetail)": a rare betta (Betta) tail with fused lobes; the line is very hard to maintain.
"Vây dính (fusefin)": an extremely rare betta (Betta) in which the dorsal, caudal and anal fins are joined.
"Cá betta đuôi nhót/ Spade tail": a small, round tail with a pointed tip; the page says it is rare in Vietnam.
"Cá betta half sun": a large tail spread at 180 degrees like a halfmoon, with a slightly split edge; the page says it is rare in Vietnam.
"Cá betta Plakat/ Vây ngắn": a short-finned, compact betta (Betta) line.
Fin and tail rot often starts with frayed fin edges and a reddened caudal fin, then greyish fin tips that erode and bleed.
Advanced fin rot can erode the fin back to the caudal peduncle and expose bone, with ulcerated tissue.
Bacterial fin rot looks whitish or grey and damages patches unevenly; fungal rot looks creamy or whitish and hairy and spreads more evenly.
Fin rot usually starts at the fin edge, with an opaque or whitish lesion edge; advanced cases show redness and inflammation.
Untreated fin rot on the tail can spread into the body as peduncle disease.

Tail biting in bettas (Betta) leaves clean, chunky bites with smooth edges in places the fish can reach and can appear within a day; fin rot has ragged, decaying edges, often with a white, grey or black border, and develops over weeks.
Fin and tail rot is linked to bacteria, mainly Aeromonas, Pseudomonas and Flavobacterium, which normally live in fish skin mucus.
Poor aquarium conditions and aggressive interactions that damage fins make fish more susceptible to fin rot.
Nearly all fin rot cases are triggered by stress, fear or poor conditions, such as parasites, overcrowding, low oxygen, bullying and poor water quality.
Predisposing factors for Aeromonas and Pseudomonas infections include low dissolved oxygen, other water quality problems, handling stress, trauma, marked temperature changes and crowding.
Vibriosis can cause bleeding and ulcers of the skin, fins and tail.
Betta (Betta) tail biting can be caused by reflections, boredom in small or bare tanks, poor water quality, strong filter current, fin-nipping tankmates and sharp decor such as rough plastic plants.
Remove the stressor first; if fin rot is caught early, this alone may be enough.
For Aeromonas or Pseudomonas infections, the main approach is to remove predisposing factors; antimicrobials are recommended if fish are dying, chosen by sensitivity testing where possible.
Kanamycin in food for fin and tail rot: 200–300 mg per 100 g of food.
Kanamycin in water for fin and tail rot: 2–5 g/L for 4–5 days, followed by a 35–50% water change.
Nalidixic acid (water-soluble) bath for fin and tail rot: 13 mg/L for 1–4 hours, repeated if needed.
Malachite green for fin and tail rot: 1–3 mg/L for up to 1 hour.
Salt bath for fin and tail rot: 10 g/L for 20–30 minutes, only for species that tolerate it; adult rainbowfish (Melanotaeniidae) tolerate up to 17 g/L and juveniles up to 12 g/L.

For advanced fin rot, the damaged fin can be trimmed under sedation with sterile scissors, and an antiseptic such as povidone-iodine applied to the clean edge; add antibiotics if the infection threatens the body.
Fins are likely to regrow after minor fin-only damage, but unlikely to when the fin rays are involved.

While a betta's (Betta) tail heals from biting, change 25–30% of the water every 3–4 days and feed a protein-rich diet; use antibacterial or antifungal medication only if a secondary infection appears.

To prevent tail biting in bettas (Betta), keep lighting moderate, keep ammonia and nitrite at zero, use gentle filtration, give plants and hiding places, avoid fin-nipping tankmates and check decor for snags.
Treating a damaged fin without finding the underlying cause is a mistake; every fin rot case should be investigated for its cause.
Trimming fins with non-sterile tools is a mistake; sterile scissors are needed.
Consider antibiotics carefully before using them, and follow the maker's instructions for commercial medications because concentrations vary.
